# Cattail Run Data Campus — Phase 1 foundation strategy: spread footings versus aggregate piers

## Situation

Ardent Vale Infrastructure LLC is building six single-storey building pads (`CR-P1` … `CR-P6`) on
the Cattail Run Data Campus in Loudoun County, Virginia. You are the structural engineer of record
for the Phase 1 foundation package. The data room is under `project/`:

* `criteria/` — the governing geotechnical, structural and concrete criteria and guide
  specifications, together with cancelled predecessor volumes you must recognise and set aside;
* `references/` — the analysis manuals the criteria point to for bearing capacity, settlement,
  lateral earth pressure and sliding, reinforced-concrete footing design, and ground modification,
  plus one manual written for a different class of structure;
* `geotech/` — the geotechnical data report, two boring logs per pad, the laboratory summary, a
  superseded addendum, an adjacent-parcel report, and, in `geotech/regional/`, real regional soil
  and climate data products;
* `structural/` — the base-reaction force vectors exported from the analytical model, the column
  grid, and the load-combination memorandum;
* `civil/` — the grading and groundwater record;
* `cost/` — the contractor bid schedule and the ground-improvement subcontractor's budget proposal;
* `owner/` — the basis of design (and its superseded revision), the authority-having-jurisdiction
  amendment letter, the RFI log, the BIM parameter standard and the schedule and register templates.

Every parameter is found in those documents. **None of them is restated here.**

Each pad carries one instrumented column line of six foundation units: five isolated column
footings and one continuous shear-wall footing. For every one of the thirty-six foundations you must
size the footing, set the reinforcement, assign the concrete, and decide whether it is carried on a
shallow spread footing alone or on a spread footing over rammed aggregate piers. All foundations on
a pad share one bearing elevation. Ground improvement is bought by the rig, not by the pad, and the
subcontractor's mobilisation and scheduling terms constrain how many pads one mobilised rig can
serve. The campus programme must be compliant at every foundation and **should cost as little as
possible** at the project unit prices.

The unit prices issued with the basis of design are project budget prices prepared for this
procurement. They are fictional for any other purpose; optimise against them as issued.

## Deliverable

A single file **`output/submission.zip`** containing exactly these six files at the archive root:

1. **`foundation_geometry.json`** — the Revit foundation geometry parameter file, in the shape and
   with the rules the owner's BIM parameter standard sets out. It is what the grader parses: every
   number in it is yours, derived from the documents.

2. **`ground_improvement_plan.json`** — the ground-improvement programme, in the shape the same BIM
   parameter standard sets out: the stress concentration ratio and pier diameter adopted, the rigs
   mobilised with the pads each one serves, the mobilisation cost, the verification-testing count
   per improved pad, and per improved pad the stiffness modulus used, the treatment depth and the
   total pier linear feet.

3. **`foundation_schedule.xlsx`** — the foundation schedule, on the owner's template, one row per
   foundation for all thirty-six, with the columns the template defines. It must agree with the
   parameter file.

4. **`foundation_feasibility_matrix.md`** — the foundation-type feasibility and optimisation matrix.
   For every pad (headed by its pad ID) and every foundation on it: the demand, the bearing check,
   the predicted settlement, the stability checks on the shear-wall footing, the constraint that
   governs, and the shallow-versus-improved decision with the cost of **both** alternatives that
   decided it.

5. **`constraint_register.xlsx`** — the register of every requirement you applied, on the owner's
   template, with the columns `req_id`, `document`, `clause`, `requirement`, `value`, `unit`,
   `kind`, `applies_to`, `resolution`. The register is scored. Register what you actually used, with
   the real document and the real clause, table or equation number. A requirement family whose
   governing clause you did not register earns no credit even if your numbers are right. Only the
   first **96 rows** are read for matching, so putting the substance first matters. Rows that cite a
   document which is not in the data room at all, and rows that cite a cancelled or superseded
   document as if it were live, reduce the register's credit; a row that cites a cancelled or
   superseded document and says in its `resolution` column that it was set aside is neutral, and so
   is any additional correct row. A register whose credit falls below 0.30 is treated as padding and
   registers nothing at all; below a credit of 0.60 the register score is scaled down in proportion.

6. **`design_basis.md`** — the design basis. It must **open with a fenced ` ```json ` block** of
   this shape, followed by the narrative:

   ```json
   {"frost": {"afi_100yr_F_days": 0, "afi_product_period": "...", "frost_depth_in": 0,
              "superseded_product_period": "...", "superseded_afi_100yr_F_days": 0},
    "pads": {"<PAD-ID>": {"governing_constraint": "...",
                          "foundation_decision": "SPREAD|IMPROVED_SPREAD",
                          "spread_only_cost_usd": 0, "improved_cost_usd": 0}},
    "campus": {"rigs_mobilised": 0, "mobilisation_cost_usd": 0, "total_cost_usd": 0,
               "pads_improved": ["..."]},
    "rejected_criteria": ["..."]}
   ```

   The narrative must state: the criteria that govern and the documents that were reviewed and set
   aside, with the reason; the bearing-capacity and settlement methods actually applied and the
   basis of the factor of safety used at each pad; the tolerable-movement criteria adopted and any
   competing criterion rejected; the ground-improvement design parameters with the authority for
   each; how every conflict between documents was resolved, with the governing value; and the
   reasoning behind the campus programme — which pads are improved, how many rigs are mobilised and
   why that number.

Keep the archive under 25 MB and 200 files.

## Grading

Pads are graded individually against the grader's own derivation from the same documents; a subset
of the pads is used for scoring. Requirement families are tagged HARD (bearing capacity and the
factor of safety, the groundwater correction, the bearing stratum, total and differential
settlement, minimum widths, frost protection, sliding, overturning and uplift of the shear-wall
footing, footing shear and reinforcement, the sulfate exposure condition and the concrete durability
limits, the aggregate-pier replacement ratio, stress ratio, stiffness modulus and treatment depth,
the mobilisation programme, and the prohibition on presumptive bearing values) or SOFT (schedule
completeness, parameter-file conformance, the verification-testing programme, and the design-basis
statements — four of which are judged by an LLM against verbatim quotes from `design_basis.md`).

### How your reported analysis values are reviewed

The grader re-derives the physics from **your own geometry** and checks that your design is safe.
Where it also compares a number you *reported*, the comparison is **one-sided and tolerant of
conservatism** — being more cautious than the grader's recomputation never costs you a family:

* a **capacity** you report may not be more permissive than the grader's recomputation by more than
  **6 %** (net allowable bearing pressure; sliding and uplift factors of safety, 20 %). Any bearing
  method at least as conservative as the general bearing-capacity equation of the governing
  foundations manual is accepted — including the least of three methods. There is **no lower bound**
  on a reported capacity;
* a **demand** you report may not fall below the grader's recomputation by more than **15 %**
  (applied net bearing pressure), **20 %** (settlement, eccentricity), **10 %** (top-of-pier
  stress). There is **no upper bound**;
* the recomputed **angular distortion between adjacent units** is graded against the criteria's own
  limit **exactly**. Both sides of that comparison are computed by the grader from your geometry
  with the settlement procedure the data room states, so no reporting band applies to it;
* required **flexural steel** is a lower bound with a **10 %** tolerance; the code minimum
  reinforcement ratios are exact;
* the recomputed **shear thickness** requirement is a lower bound evaluated with the most permissive
  strength-reduction factor in general use, so a footing designed by the shipped manual's own worked
  examples is thicker than required;
* the one-sided bands have a **sanity floor**: a reported net allowable bearing pressure may not
  fall below **half** the grader's recomputation (the least of three widely accepted methods is
  about 0.82 × of it, so the floor is more than three times clear of the most conservative method
  the criteria invite), and a reported settlement may not exceed the total-settlement limit you are
  designing to. Neither test costs a conservative solver anything;
* the **hard limits themselves are exact**: the total-settlement limit, the minimum footing widths,
  the minimum factors of safety, the exposure classes and the concrete limits, the
  replacement-ratio, top-of-pier-stress and treatment-depth bounds, and the owner's dimensioning
  grid and minimum footing thickness.

The governing constraint you name for a pad is accepted if it is a constraint that **selects** that
pad's design: either taking one 3-in step of plan width off any one foundation on the pad (with that
footing's shear thickness re-derived at the smaller width) would violate it, or your **own reported**
bearing, settlement or differential-settlement numbers put it at **80 %** or more of its limit
somewhere on the pad. Footing thickness and bearing elevation are dependent variables of this
problem - the thickness follows from shear and the elevation from frost - so `PUNCHING_SHEAR` is not
a pad-level governing constraint, and `FROST` is accepted only where the pad is founded at the frost
minimum and nothing else on it is near binding. All nine values remain legal per foundation in the
parameter file.

Per pad: a family earns credit only if it is **both** satisfied **and** registered. Let `p` be
the fraction of all 32 families satisfied-and-registered, multiplied by the register precision factor
described above, and `h` the fraction of the 22 HARD families satisfied-and-registered (not multiplied
by that factor). Let `O` be the programme credit = (a certified lower
bound on the cost of any compliant campus programme) / (the grader's repricing of **your** design
at the project unit prices), capped at 1.

The pad score is `0.4 p + 0.6 [h = 1] O'`, where `O' = clip((O - O_naive) / (1 - O_naive), 0, 1)` and
`O_naive` is the programme credit of a naive baseline programme. Thus a parseable pad earns programme
credit (none when the design cannot be repriced) only when all of its HARD families are
satisfied-and-registered (`h = 1`): an omitted citation or a physical
HARD violation forfeits the programme credit. A missing or
unparseable pad scores 0. The task score is the mean over the graded pads.

The lower bound comes from a relaxation of the campus problem, so the programme credit is strictly
below 1 for every attainable design; a cheaper compliant programme never scores worse than a more
expensive one, and the grader reprices your own decisions, so a programme that under-buys
mobilisations or misstates a quantity is repriced at what it actually costs. Reinforcement is priced
at the greater of the ratio you report and the ratio your design actually requires, so the tolerance
on the flexural steel cannot be spent on cost.

documents alone and submit your best final deliverable; it will be graded offline by the
frozen verifier on held-out instances.

   is any additional correct row. A register whose credit falls below 0.30 is treated as padding and
   registers nothing at all; below a credit of 0.60 the register score is scaled down in proportion.

6. **`design_basis.md`** — the design basis. It must **open with a fenced ` ```json ` block** of
   this shape, followed by the narrative:

   ```json
   {"frost": {"afi_100yr_F_days": 0, "afi_product_period": "...", "frost_depth_in": 0,
              "superseded_product_period": "...", "superseded_afi_100yr_F_days": 0},
    "pads": {"<PAD-ID>": {"governing_constraint": "...",
                          "foundation_decision": "SPREAD|IMPROVED_SPREAD",
                          "spread_only_cost_usd": 0, "improved_cost_usd": 0}},
    "campus": {"rigs_mobilised": 0, "mobilisation_cost_usd": 0, "total_cost_usd": 0,
               "pads_improved": ["..."]},
    "rejected_criteria": ["..."]}
   ```

   The narrative must state: the criteria that govern and the documents that were reviewed and set
   aside, with the reason; the bearing-capacity and settlement methods actually applied and the
   basis of the factor of safety used at each pad; the tolerable-movement criteria adopted and any
   competing criterion rejected; the ground-improvement design parameters with the authority for
   each; how every conflict between documents was resolved, with the governing value; and the
   reasoning behind the campus programme — which pads are improved, how many rigs are mobilised and
   why that number.

Keep the archive under 25 MB and 200 files.

## Grading

Pads are graded individually against the grader's own derivation from the same documents; a subset
of the pads is used for scoring. Requirement families are tagged HARD (bearing capacity and the
factor of safety, the groundwater correction, the bearing stratum, total and differential
settlement, minimum widths, frost protection, sliding, overturning and uplift of the shear-wall
footing, footing shear and reinforcement, the sulfate exposure condition and the concrete durability
limits, the aggregate-pier replacement ratio, stress ratio, stiffness modulus and treatment depth,
the mobilisation programme, and the prohibition on presumptive bearing values) or SOFT (schedule
completeness, parameter-file conformance, the verification-testing programme, and the design-basis
statements — four of which are judged by an LLM against verbatim quotes from `design_basis.md`).

### How your reported analysis values are reviewed

The grader re-derives the physics from **your own geometry** and checks that your design is safe.
Where it also compares a number you *reported*, the comparison is **one-sided and tolerant of
conservatism** — being more cautious than the grader's recomputation never costs you a family:

* a **capacity** you report may not be more permissive than the grader's recomputation by more than
  **6 %** (net allowable bearing pressure; sliding and uplift factors of safety, 20 %). Any bearing
  method at least as conservative as the general bearing-capacity equation of the governing
  foundations manual is accepted — including the least of three methods. There is **no lower bound**
  on a reported capacity;
* a **demand** you report may not fall below the grader's recomputation by more than **15 %**
  (applied net bearing pressure), **20 %** (settlement, eccentricity), **10 %** (top-of-pier
  stress). There is **no upper bound**;
* the recomputed **angular distortion between adjacent units** is graded against the criteria's own
  limit **exactly**. Both sides of that comparison are computed by the grader from your geometry
  with the settlement procedure the data room states, so no reporting band applies to it;
* required **flexural steel** is a lower bound with a **10 %** tolerance; the code minimum
  reinforcement ratios are exact;
* the recomputed **shear thickness** requirement is a lower bound evaluated with the most permissive
  strength-reduction factor in general use, so a footing designed by the shipped manual's own worked
  examples is thicker than required;
* the one-sided bands have a **sanity floor**: a reported net allowable bearing pressure may not
  fall below **half** the grader's recomputation (the least of three widely accepted methods is
  about 0.82 × of it, so the floor is more than three times clear of the most conservative method
  the criteria invite), and a reported settlement may not exceed the total-settlement limit you are
  designing to. Neither test costs a conservative solver anything;
* the **hard limits themselves are exact**: the total-settlement limit, the minimum footing widths,
  the minimum factors of safety, the exposure classes and the concrete limits, the
  replacement-ratio, top-of-pier-stress and treatment-depth bounds, and the owner's dimensioning
  grid and minimum footing thickness.

The governing constraint you name for a pad is accepted if it is a constraint that **selects** that
pad's design: either taking one 3-in step of plan width off any one foundation on the pad (with that
footing's shear thickness re-derived at the smaller width) would violate it, or your **own reported**
bearing, settlement or differential-settlement numbers put it at **80 %** or more of its limit
somewhere on the pad. Footing thickness and bearing elevation are dependent variables of this
problem - the thickness follows from shear and the elevation from frost - so `PUNCHING_SHEAR` is not
a pad-level governing constraint, and `FROST` is accepted only where the pad is founded at the frost
minimum and nothing else on it is near binding. All nine values remain legal per foundation in the
parameter file.

Per pad: a family earns credit only if it is **both** satisfied **and** registered. Let `p` be
the fraction of all 32 families satisfied-and-registered, multiplied by the register precision factor
described above, and `h` the fraction of the 22 HARD families satisfied-and-registered (not multiplied
by that factor). Let `O` be the programme credit = (a certified lower
bound on the cost of any compliant campus programme) / (the grader's repricing of **your** design
at the project unit prices), capped at 1.

The pad score is `0.4 p + 0.6 [h = 1] O'`, where `O' = clip((O - O_naive) / (1 - O_naive), 0, 1)` and
`O_naive` is the programme credit of a naive baseline programme. Thus a parseable pad earns programme
credit (none when the design cannot be repriced) only when all of its HARD families are
satisfied-and-registered (`h = 1`): an omitted citation or a physical
HARD violation forfeits the programme credit. A missing or
unparseable pad scores 0. The task score is the mean over the graded pads.

The lower bound comes from a relaxation of the campus problem, so the programme credit is strictly
below 1 for every attainable design; a cheaper compliant programme never scores worse than a more
expensive one, and the grader reprices your own decisions, so a programme that under-buys
mobilisations or misstates a quantity is repriced at what it actually costs. Reinforcement is priced
at the greater of the ratio you report and the ratio your design actually requires, so the tolerance
on the flexural steel cannot be spent on cost.


## Verifier access (blind variant)

No verifier, oracle, or evaluation data of any kind is available in this workspace — the
only checks you can run are the ones you build yourself. Work from the brief and the
documents alone and submit your best final deliverable; it will be graded offline by the
frozen verifier on held-out instances.

# Cattail Run Data Campus - BIM foundation parameter standard (Rev. 2)

The foundation geometry parameter file is consumed directly by the Revit family generator.  It is a
single UTF-8 JSON object named `foundation_geometry.json` with this shape:

```json
{"project": {"campus_total_cost_usd": 0.0, "frost_depth_in": 0, "afi_100yr_F_days": 0},
 "pads": {"<PAD-ID>": {
     "bearing_depth_in": 0, "fs_bearing": 0.0, "occupancy_class": "...",
     "improved": false, "sulfate_pct": 0.0, "sulfate_exposure_class": "S0|S1|S2",
     "exposure_classes": ["..."], "fc_psi": 0, "max_wcm": 0.0, "dewatering_days": 0,
     "governing_constraint": "...",
     "foundations": {"<TAG>": {
         "foundation_type": "SPREAD|IMPROVED_SPREAD",
         "B_in": 0, "L_in": 0, "thickness_in": 0, "bearing_stratum": "I|II|III",
         "reinforcement_ratio": 0.0, "bar_size": 4, "bar_spacing_in": 12,
         "q_net_ksf": 0.0, "q_allow_net_ksf": 0.0, "settlement_in": 0.0,
         "pier_count": 0, "pier_diameter_in": 0, "pier_depth_ft": 0,
         "area_replacement_ratio": 0.0, "top_of_pier_stress_psf": 0.0,
         "governing_constraint": "..."}}}}}
```

Rules the generator enforces:

* every one of the six pads and every one of its six foundations must be present;
* `B_in`, `L_in`, `thickness_in` and `bearing_depth_in` are NUMBERS in inches, dimensioned to the
  nearest 3 in; `pier_depth_ft` is a whole number of feet; `pier_count` is a whole number;
* no `null` values anywhere; a spread footing carries zeros in the pier fields;
* `bearing_depth_in` is identical for every foundation on a pad and is repeated once at pad level;
* `governing_constraint` is one of `BEARING`, `SETTLEMENT`, `ANGULAR_DISTORTION`, `MIN_WIDTH`,
  `SLIDING`, `OVERTURNING`, `UPLIFT`, `PUNCHING_SHEAR`, `FROST`;
* the shear-wall foundation of each pad additionally carries `sliding_fs`, `eccentricity_in` and
  `uplift_fs`.

The ground-improvement plan is a separate JSON object named `ground_improvement_plan.json`:

```json
{"stress_concentration_ratio_ns": 0.0, "pier_diameter_in": 0,
 "rigs_mobilised": 0, "mobilisation_cost_usd": 0.0, "pads_improved": ["..."],
 "rig_assignments": {"RIG-1": ["<PAD-ID>", "..."]},
 "modulus_tests": {"<PAD-ID>": 0},
 "pads": {"<PAD-ID>": {"stiffness_modulus_pci": 0.0, "treatment_depth_ft": 0,
                       "total_pier_lf": 0.0}}}
```

`treatment_depth_ft` at pad level is the deepest treatment depth used on that pad.

1.   Abstract: A climatography of the Air-freezing Index (AFI) has been 
developed for 3,110 stations in the United States and is presented here as a 
digital data set.  The AFI is a measure of the combined magnitude and duration 
of air temperatures above and below freezing during any given winter season.  
The AFI, the thermal properties of the soil, and the surface soil cover are 
the major parameters used to determine the ground freezing potential of a 
given climate.   
 
Data Set Overview: 
 
This data set consists of two statistics stored as separate records within 
this data-set file.  The first statistic represents the computation of 29 
seasonal AFI totals for each winter season that occurred during the 1951-1980 
period.  These winter season AFI totals were computed separately for each 
climate station.  The second statistic represents an estimate of various 
return periods of the AFI for each station using the 29 seasonal totals for 
that station as input. The return periods included in this data set are 1.1-
years, 1.25 years, 2-years, 2.5-years, 3.3-years, 5-years, 10-years, 20-years, 
25-years, 50-years, and 100-years.  A return period is defined as a measure of 
the average amount of time between which an event of a given magnitude will be 
equaled or exceeded (Gumbel, 1958). Thus, a 100-year return period of the AFI, 
as an example, would be equaled or exceeded once every 100 years on average.  
 
Work by Steurer (1985, 1989) used serially complete daily maximum and minimum 
temperature data from 1951-1980 to generate the 29 seasonal totals of the AFI 
for 3,110 stations in the United States.  A detailed description of the 
computation procedures used to generate the AFI is presented by Steurer and 
Crandell (1995) along with a graph that depicts a sinusoidal cumulative AFI 
curve for a typical mid-latitude station. See References.  
 
Generally, the daily AFI is defined as the departure of the daily mean 
temperature above or below 32 degrees Fahrenheit.  The daily AFI departures 
are then summed each day throughout the freezing season and plotted as a 
cumulative AFI total.  A freezing season is defined as beginning on August 1 
and ending on July 31 of the next year.  Starting at zero, the daily AFI 
cumulative curve for a typical mid-latitude station would become positive and 
turn upward at the beginning of the freezing season when the daily average 
temperature was above freezing, then become negative and turn downward as 
daily average temperatures consistently dropped below 32 degrees Fahrenheit in 
the Winter, and then turn upward again in the Spring or Summer when daily mean 
temperature consistently was above freezing.  The AFI for a winter season is 
defined as the difference between the highest and lowest inflection points on 
this cumulative time curve of daily AFI departures.  However, for sites that 
do not exhibit a typical four-season climate such as in the Southern United 
States, there may not be a well-defined cumulative AFI time curve.  Instead 
there may be several maxima and minima that correspond to cold outbreaks that 
occur throughout the winter months.  Since each cold outbreak is essentially a 
separate event for these warmer climate stations, only the difference between 
the maximum and its corresponding minimum of the largest cold outbreak event 
is assigned the seasonal AFI total.  
 
Data Applications 
 
When the temperature remains below freezing for a period of time, ice lenses 
can form in the soil that result in frost heave and possible damage to 
overlying structures (Jones et al., 1982).  Structural damages caused by frost 
action in soils are most notable in the pavement of highways and airfields, in 

: 
: 
 
4:
hydraulic structures such as dams and canals, and in residential and 
commercial buildings.  An important application of the AFI is the estimation 
of the effect of freezing conditions upon the soil foundations of structures. 
In non-permafrost environments, a conventional method of controlling frost 
action in soils is to locate a structural foundation below the depth of frost 
penetration.  The depth of frost penetration has empirically been determined 
by using the AFI in conjunction with the soil type and surface soil cover 
(Linell and Lobacz, 1980). 
 
A frost-protected shallow foundation (FPSF) is another method used to protect 
structural foundations from frost heave (Farouki 1992; Morris 1988).  FPSF 
incorporates the strategic placement of insulation to raise the frost depth 
around a building, thereby allowing foundations as shallow as 0.4 meters (16 
inches), even in the most severe climates.  The amount of insulation required 
to protect a foundation has been found to be a function of the AFI ("Frost" 
1993).  Cost savings to the buyer of new homes using FPSF have been estimated 
to range from 1 to 4 percent over the cost of conventional slab-on-grade 
construction or an annual savings of $300 million nationally.  Additional 
long-term savings are expected from increased energy efficiency ("Frost” 
1994).   
 
Description of the AFI Return Period Estimates 
 
Various statistics can be used to represent the AFI.  The ones more commonly 
used in the United States are the mean, the design value (Jones et al., 1982), 
and the 100-year return period (Steurer, 1989).  The mean is a measure of 
average conditions and is simply the average of the seasonal AFI totals for 
ten or more winter seasons.  Jones et al. (1982) indicate that the mean index 
is used primarily in the construction phase of temporary structures.  For more 
permanent structures, the design AFI can be used.  Here, the seasonal totals 
for the three coldest winters in a 30-year period are averaged.  To provide an 
index that reflects conditions during the coldest winter seasons, work by 
Steurer (1989) resulted in the development of an estimate of the 100-year 
return period of the AFI using the Weibull probability distribution. 
 
A total of 29 seasonal totals of the AFI was computed at each climate station 
and used to compute an estimate of the 100-year return period for that 
station.  These statistics were produced for 3,110 stations in the United 
States based upon the period 1951-1980.  A return period is defined as a 
measure of the average amount of time between which an event of a given 
magnitude will be equaled or exceeded (Gumbel, 1958).  A return period is 
described by the equation 1/p where p is the probability of the event 
occurring over a specified period of time.  Using this equation, a 2-year 
return period of the AFI would occur on average in 50% of the years (1/.5), 
while a 100-year  return  period would occur on average in only 1% of the 
years (1/.01).  A common misuse of return periods is to expect, as an example, 
the 100-year return period to occur exactly every 100 years.  It is quite 
possible to equal or exceed the 100-year return period of the AFI in two 
successive years or not reach it in more than 500 years.  But when the average 
is considered, the length of time between events will be 100 years for a valid 
100-year return period estimate (Linsley et al., 1949). 
 
Different methods have been used to obtain an estimate of the AFI for other 
locations around the world.  Different AFI computation procedures have been 
performed for locations in Norway (Heiersted, 1976) and Finland (Anderson, 
personal communication, 1993).  Work by Steurer and Crandell (1995) 
investigated the differences among the USA method, which used return periods, 

: 
: 
 
5:
and Norway, and Finland methods.  They found that the USA method was more 
representative of the freezing effect for all U.S. climate regimes.  This was 
in terms of calculating an unbiased AFI that considered all freezing and 
thawing events during the winter regardless of their duration or time of 
occurrence.  As a result of this work, U.S. building codes as regulated by the 
1995 Edition of the Council of Building Officials (CABO) One and Two-Family 
Dwelling Code were changed to accept FPSF as a mechanism to offset increased 
construction costs and provide more energy-efficient housing (Crandell, 
personal communication, 1994). 
 
However, Steurer and Crandell (1995) pointed out that there were potential 
shortcomings in fitting one probability distribution to every possible climate 
regime, especially when the sample size was relatively small (Kite, 1977).   
To address the problem of a small sample size, a longer-term data set was used 
in another study performed by Steurer (1996) that contained temperature data 
for 1901-1987.  This 138-station network of U.S. observing sites is considered 
by some climate researchers to be a high quality and long-term temperature 
data sets in terms of temporal homogeneity and spatial coverage (Hughes et al, 
1992).  A total of 25 of the 138 available stations were selected for this 
study.  The stations that were chosen had few missing data and also maintained 
the same observation time throughout the 1901-1987 period.  This resulted in a 
sample size of 86 winter seasons or data points for each station.  This latter 
work revealed that the Weibull probability distribution was still determined 
as the best choice for use in estimating the 100-year return period of the AFI 
for all U.S. climate regimes.

the design load.  Designs that exceed it will not be warranted.  Treatment depth is measured below the

The spacing of the stone columns may be determined using Figure 5-23 to determine the

4.1.3.3 Permeability 
In order to avoid significant generation of pore water pressures within the stone column, it is 
recommended that the permeability of the stone column be at least two orders of magnitude 
larger than the treated soil. This recommendation can be achieved by selection of the 
gradation for the stone column, with due regard to piping considerations outlined below. 
4.1.3.4 Piping Prevention 
There is a likelihood that hydraulic gradients may exceed critical gradients (greater than one). 
This situation may initiate a movement of fines from the natural soil into the large, open pore 
structure of the stone column during seismic loading, leading to the development of cavities 
within the soil structure and potentially undesirable volume change. In reality, due to the 
short duration of the strong motion, it is unlikely that much soil material could be carried into 
the stone column.

4.2.1 Design Considerations 
The design concept used for rammed aggregate piers is almost identical to that used for stone

For area wide ground improvement applications, the design method is identical to that 
previously detailed for stone columns. The stone within the rammed aggregate piers having 
been compacted by impact ramming typically exhibits a somewhat higher effective friction 
angle, in the range of 45 to 50 degrees, and potentially higher stiffness (modulus). 
Consequently, the ratio of the stiffness (modulus) of the rammed aggregate piers to the 
stiffness of the in situ soil should be somewhat higher than for stone columns, resulting in a 
higher design stress ratio than previously identified for stone columns. Although the Geopier 
design manual suggests stress ratios of 20 or higher, a stress ratio of 5 to 10 for area ground 
improvement applications under flexible embankment loading appears warranted until 
considerably more field data in support of a higher ratio is developed. 
For structure foundation support under rigid footings a somewhat higher stress ratio (10) may 
be considered, with anticipated settlements and pier capacity conventionally computed, based 
on the loads on each element. The load on the rammed aggregate pier and on the in situ soil 
is based on the chosen stress and replacement ratios. The design area replacement ratio is 
determined after evaluating settlement of the unimproved soil. A minimum replacement ratio 
of 0.33 is generally recommended, as noted in the HITEC Evaluation Report (Collin 2007). 
4.2.2 Design Procedures 
Rammed aggregate piers are typically selected to increase bearing resistance, reduce 
settlement, increase shear strength, or provide any combination of the above. 
Preliminary design methods and assumptions to achieve the desired end result are outlined in 
this section. 
The generalized design process for an embankment support is as follows: 
1. Perform embankment design without rammed aggregate piers to determine the overall 
settlement and global stability to determine if rammed aggregate piers or another 
form of ground improvement are required. If so proceed to step 2. 
2. Assume an area replacement ratio and column diameter. 
3. Determine the spacing based on the assumed area replacement ratio and column 
diameter.  
4. Check the load bearing resistance of the rammed aggregate pier to see if it meets the 
project requirements. If not revise the column diameter and re-check. 
5. Determine the total settlement of the embankment supported on rammed aggregate 
piers.

Design Verification 
As an important adjunct to design, a field verification program of load tests and in situ testing 
must be developed and implemented through appropriate construction specification 
requirements. A program should be specified, regardless of the contracting method. 
A combination of load tests on aggregate columns constructed before, during, and after 
production should be specified to verify the design assumptions and the performance 
specification. There are three types of load tests: (1) short-term tests, which are used to 
evaluate ultimate stone column bearing resistance, (2) long-term tests, which are used to 
measure the consolidation settlement characteristics; and (3) horizontal or composite shear 
tests, which are used to evaluate the composite aggregate-soil shear strength for use in

stability analyses. The most common of these tests is the short-term load test on a single 
column. 
The short-term load tests, similar to pile load tests, should be performed after all excess pore 
pressures induced during construction have been dissipated. The load increment should 
closely correspond to the actual loading. For example, if the actual foundation load will be 
applied very slowly, a load increment of approximately 10 percent of the ultimate should be 
used. A rapid loading may result in immediate settlement, as well as consolidation 
settlement. If the actual load will be applied rapidly, a load increment of 20 to 25 percent of 
ultimate should be used. The tests are generally performed to 150% of the design load, and 
the measured settlement is compared to project settlement tolerance. For example, a final 
acceptance criterion of 1 inch of settlement at 150 to 200 percent of the design load appears 
to be a reasonable criterion for columns supporting a structure. 
The long-term settlement of the stone column foundation is usually estimated from the 
results of short-term load tests on single stone columns. Mitchell (1981) reported that the 
foundation settlement due to a uniform loading of a large area was 5 to 10 times greater than 
the settlement measured in a short-term load test on a single column. However, there is very 
little field data available to confirm this behavior. Therefore, it is recommended that long-
term load tests on a group of columns be conducted in conjunction with short-term load tests 
to develop an estimate of the settlement of the stone column foundation. The long-term load 
tests should be conducted on a minimum of three to four stone columns located within a 
group of 9 to 12 columns having the proposed spacing and pattern. The load should be 
applied over the tributary area of the columns and left in place until the cohesive soil reaches 
a primary degree of consolidation of 90-95 percent. The applied load could consist of column 
backfill material, native material, and/or the dead weight from the short-term load tests. The 
results of these tests will provide valuable information for estimating the ultimate settlement 
of the stone column foundation. 
During the production phase of construction, a few short-term load tests can be performed for 
quality control purposes. These tests are referred to as proof tests and are used to verify 
quality control during production. The load applied in the proof test is usually 150 to 200 
percent of the allowable/design load.

BEARING CAPACITY OF SOIL AND ROCK. 
 
Bearing Capacity Theory. 
The ultimate bearing capacity can be defined as the highest applied stress that the soil 
or rock withstands at the point of plastic failure.  As developed by Terzaghi (1943), 
ultimate bearing capacity considers two types of failure.   
General shear failure occurs along a well-defined failure surface below and beyond the 
edges of a footing as shown in Figure 5-3(a).  The triangular Zone I under the footing in 
Figure 5-3 acts as though it is part of the footing, and the soil remains in an elastic state.  
For a vertical load, the major principal stress is aligned vertically in Zone I.  In Zone III, 
the soil reaches a state of Rankine passive earth pressure with the major principal 
stress aligned horizontally.  Zone II is known as the zone of radial shear, which allows 
the stress system to rotate between Zones I and III. 
General shear failure normally occurs in a dense coarse-grained or very stiff cohesive 
soil.  At failure, the soil on both sides of the footing bulges and the footing may rotate.  A 
state of plastic equilibrium is reached in Zones II and III in this type of failure.  General 
shear failure can be catastrophic for large mat supported structures although individual 
footings rarely experience this type of failure.  Dense and very stiff soils generally 
experience relatively low settlements at typical allowable bearing pressures. 

*** PDF PAGE 322 (Doc page 284) ***
UFC 3-220-20 
16 January 2025 
 
 
284 
 
Figure 5-3 
Bearing Capacity Failure Modes – (a) General Shear, (b) Local Shear, 
(c) Load-Settlement Behavior, and (d) Effect of Relative Density on Failure Mode 
(after Das 2022, Terzaghi 1943, Vesic 1973) 
Local shear failure occurs when the soil in Zone II compresses rather than developing a 
plastic shear state as shown in Figure 5-3(b).  For this reason, the soil in Zone III is not 
engaged in the failure mechanism.  Individual shear failure surfaces typically do not 
reach the ground surface.  Failure is not sudden, and tilting does not occur.  
Settlements are usually substantial, and plastic equilibrium is only partially developed.   
As shown in Figure 5-3(c), the dense or stiff soils associated with general shear failure 
develop qult at low strain or settlement.  The ultimate bearing capacity is well-defined.  In 
constrast, the local shear mechanism in loose or soft soils results in large strains and 
settlements.  Because much of the movement is associated with the compressibility of 
the soil, the magnitude of qult is much less distinct.   
Punching shear is dominated by compression of the soil below and vertical shear along 
the sides of the footing (Vesic 1973).  Little to no movement occurs in the soil adjacent 

*** PDF PAGE 323 (Doc page 285) ***
UFC 3-220-20 
16 January 2025 
 
 
285 
to the footing.  Considerations of settlement will control when punching shear is the 
dominant bearing capacity failure mode.  The term punching shear is also used by 
some to refer to the case of a footing punching through a thin layer of stiff consistency 
or dense soil into a soft consistency or loose soil below.  This mechanism is discussed 
in Section 5-3.6.  
As indicated by Figure 5-3(d), the general shear mechanism applies mostly to dense 
soils at relatively shallow depths.  At lower relative densities and greater footing depths, 
the failure mode transitions through local failure to punching shear.  The bearing 
capacity theories discussed in Section 5-3.1.2 assume a general shear failure 
mechanism.  Methods to account for local shear are discussed in Section 5-3.1.3.  
5-3.1.1 
Shear Strength for Bearing Capacity Analysis. 
Bearing capacity is controlled by the shear strength of the soil.  The type of shear 
strength parameters used in bearing capacity analyses depends on the field loading 
condition, soil type, and groundwater level.  Loads are typically applied to foundations 
over a period of time, such as when a building or a bridge is under construction.  This 
loading condition may represent drained or undrained loading depending on the type of 
soil being loaded and the length of time required to apply the load.   
In clean sands and gravels, drainage is almost instantaneous and does not practically 
depend on how long it takes to build the structure.  These soils only require effective 
stress analysis unless dynamic loading is anticipated.  If substantial fines are present, 
the possibility of developing an undrained condition should be considered. 
In contrast, substantial time is required for excess pore pressures to dissipate in fine-
grained soils after loading.  These soils usually require undrained analysis for conditions 
at the end of loading as well as for any rapid or dynamic loading.  In some cases, long-
term effective stress conditions should also be checked.  For example, the drained 
bearing capacity of heavily overconsolidated clays often controls the design. 
Laboratory and field testing methods to determine shear strength parameters for most 
soil types are summarized in the Prologue.  For bearing capacity analysis, effective 
strength parameters (φ ʹ, cʹ) should be used for long-term conditions in all soil types.  For 
saturated fine-grained soils, the use of undrained shear strength (su) with φ = 0 is 
appropriate.  Undrained shear strength parameters (φ, c) should be used for unsaturated 
soils with low permeability, including coarse-grained soils with substantial fines. 
5-3.1.2 
Calculation of Ultimate Bearing Capacity. 
Bearing capacity is a complex phenomenon that cannot be modeled exactly.  Multiple 
equations have been developed to estimate the ultimate bearing capacity of soil.  These 
equations are based on the upper and lower bound theorems of plasticity and include 

*** PDF PAGE 324 (Doc page 286) ***
UFC 3-220-20 
16 January 2025 
 
 
286 
the work of Prandtl (1920), Terzaghi (1943), Meyerhof (1951), Brinch Hansen (1970), 
and Vesic (1973, 1975).  In their basic form, the equations apply to general shear failure 
below a continuous strip footing of width, B, with soil shear strength governed by the 
Mohr-Coulomb failure criterion.  The basic bearing capacity solutions also assume 
vertical loading, a horizontal bearing surface, foundation depth less than the width, and 
a horizontal ground surface.  Methods to address other variations of these factors are 
discussed in Section 5-3.3. 
In most methods, the bearing capacity problem is simplified by replacing the soil above 
the bearing elevation with an equivalent surcharge as shown in Figure 5-4(a).  This 
conservatively neglects the shear strength of the soil above the foundation depth.  
Alternatively, Meyerhof (1951) assumed that the failure surface continued to the ground 
surface and replaced the triangular wedge with equivalent stresses, p0 and s0.  
Meyerhof’s geometry is shown in Figure 5-4(b).  Basic formulations also assume that 
the groundwater table is deeper than the failure zone. 

*** PDF PAGE 325 (Doc page 287) ***
UFC 3-220-20 
16 January 2025 
 
 
287 
 
Figure 5-4 
Assumptions for Bearing Capacity of a Continuous Footing -  
a) Terzaghi, Brinch Hansen, and Vesic Methods and b) Meyerhof Method 
With these assumptions, the bearing capacity problem can be separated into three 
distinct terms or superimposed sources of bearing resistance.  The first term is 
connected to the cohesion (or undrained shear strength) along the failure surface and 
has a bearing capacity factor, Nc.  The second term is related to the surcharge and has 
a bearing capacity factor, Nq.  The third term is related to the weight of the soil above 
the failure surface and has a bearing capacity factor, Nγ.

Bearing Capacity Corrections for Local and Punching Shear. 
As noted in the introduction to this section, the bearing capacity theories assume a 
general shear failure mode, which is only appropriate for dense and/or stiff soils.  For 
most soils, a local or punching shear mechanism is more appropriate.  In these cases, 
settlement considerations will almost always control the allowable bearing pressure and 
an accurate determination of the ultimate bearing capacity is less important.  A variety 
of methods to approximate local shear have been proposed.  A few of the more 
common approaches are summarized in Table 5-4.

Groundwater correction is required when the groundwater table is higher than one 
footing width below the bearing elevation.  Groundwater correction is only required for 
drained (effective stress) analysis.  Groundwater is considered by changing the unit

import math

phi_deg = 26.0
phi = math.radians(phi_deg)
c = 0.25 # ksf (250 psf)
gamma_total = 118.0 / 1000.0 # 0.118 ksf
gamma_sub = (118.0 - 62.4) / 1000.0 # 0.0556 ksf
Df = 3.5 # ft (42 in)

# N factors
# Nq = tan^2(45 + phi/2) * exp(pi * tan(phi))
Nq = (math.tan(math.radians(45.0 + phi_deg / 2.0)))**2 * math.exp(math.pi * math.tan(phi))
Nc = (Nq - 1.0) / math.tan(phi)
Ngamma_Hansen = 1.5 * (Nq - 1.0) * math.tan(phi)
Ngamma_Meyerhof = (Nq - 1.0) * math.tan(1.4 * phi)
# Terzaghi factors from Table 5-2: for phi=26, Nc=27, Nq=14, Ngamma=11
print(f'phi={phi_deg}: Nc={Nc:.2f}, Nq={Nq:.2f}, Ngamma_Hansen={Ngamma_Hansen:.2f}, Ngamma_Meyerhof={Ngamma_Meyerhof:.2f}')

def calc_qall_hansen(B, L, Df, Dw, FS):
    # Groundwater correction
    # sigma_zD
    if Dw >= Df:
        sigma_zD = gamma_total * Df
    else:
        sigma_zD = gamma_total * Dw + gamma_sub * (Df - Dw)
    
    # gamma for 0.5 * gamma * B * Ngamma
    if Dw >= Df + B:
        gamma_eff = gamma_total
    elif Dw <= Df:
        gamma_eff = gamma_sub
    else:
        d = Dw - Df
        gamma_eff = gamma_sub + (d / B) * (gamma_total - gamma_sub)
    
    k = Df / B if Df / B <= 1.0 else math.atan(Df / B)
    sq = 1.0 + (B / L) * math.sin(phi)
    sgamma = 1.0 - 0.4 * (B / L)
    sc = 1.0 + (B / L) * (Nq / Nc) * math.cos(phi)
    
    dq = 1.0 + 2.0 * k * math.tan(phi) * (1.0 - math.sin(phi))**2
    dc = 1.0 + k * ((1.0 - math.sin(phi))**2) * (Nq / Nc)
    dgamma = 1.0
    
    psi_c = sc * dc
    psi_q = sq * dq
    psi_gamma = sgamma * dgamma

    return q_ult, q_all_net

import math, csv

# Let's write a script to evaluate cost for any footing configuration
# Bid schedule prices
# concrete prices:
# 3000: 182, 4000: 196, 4500: 211, 5000: 228
# rebar: 1.42 / lb
# steel weight = 2 * rho * V_gross * 490 pcf
# exc: 38 / CY, backfill: 46 / CY
# exc prism = (B + 2) * (L + 2) * Df
# backfill = exc - conc
# piers: 28 / LF
# platform: 2.40 / SY
# modulus test: 9500 / improved pad

def calc_foundation_cost(B_ft, L_ft, t_in, Df_ft, rho, fc_psi, is_improved, pier_count=0, pier_depth_ft=0):
    conc_prices = {3000: 182.0, 4000: 196.0, 4500: 211.0, 5000: 228.0}
    c_price = conc_prices[fc_psi]
    
    t_ft = t_in / 12.0
    v_conc_cf = B_ft * L_ft * t_ft
    v_conc_cy = v_conc_cf / 27.0
    cost_conc = v_conc_cy * c_price
    
    w_steel_lb = 2.0 * rho * v_conc_cf * 490.0
    cost_steel = w_steel_lb * 1.42
    
    v_exc_cf = (B_ft + 2.0) * (L_ft + 2.0) * Df_ft
    v_exc_cy = v_exc_cf / 27.0
    cost_exc = v_exc_cy * 38.0
    
    v_bf_cy = max(0.0, v_exc_cy - v_conc_cy)
    cost_bf = v_bf_cy * 46.0
    
    cost_piers = pier_count * pier_depth_ft * 28.0 if is_improved else 0.0
    cost_platform = (B_ft * L_ft / 9.0) * 2.40 if is_improved else 0.0
    
    total = cost_conc + cost_steel + cost_exc + cost_bf + cost_piers + cost_platform
    return {
        'total': total,
        'conc': cost_conc,
        'steel': cost_steel,
        'exc': cost_exc,
        'bf': cost_bf,
        'piers': cost_piers,
        'platform': cost_platform
    }

print('Cost calculation function ready.')
"

def calc_settlement_unimproved(P, B, L, base_I, base_II, Es):
    q_net = P / (B * L)
    z_max = max(4.0 * B, 40.0)
    H = 0.25
    n_layers = int(math.ceil(z_max / H))
    total_s = 0.0
    for i in range(n_layers):
        z_mid = (i + 0.5) * H
        if z_mid > z_max:
            break
        d_sigma = (q_net * B * L) / ((B + z_mid) * (L + z_mid))
        depth = Df + z_mid
        if depth <= base_I:
            E = Es['I']
        elif depth <= base_II:
            E = Es['II']
        else:
            E = Es['III']
        total_s += (d_sigma * H) / E
    return total_s * 12.0

def size_spread_pad(pad):
    pdata = borings[pad]
    footings = {}
    for tag in ['F1', 'F2', 'F3', 'F4', 'F5', 'W1']:
        P_serv = reactions[(pad, tag)]['SERVICE_D_PLUS_L']['P']
        Pu = reactions[(pad, tag)]['STRENGTH_1.2D_1.6L']['P']
        sta = stations[tag]
        base_I = round(pdata['A'] + (pdata['B'] - pdata['A']) * (sta / 77.0), 1)
        base_II = round(base_I + pdata['II'], 1)
        
        min_B_in = 21 if tag == 'W1' else 24
        best = None
        for B_in in range(min_B_in, 480, 3):
            B = B_in / 12.0
            L = 24.0 if tag == 'W1' else B
            q_all = calc_qall(B, L, Df, pdata['Dw'], pdata['FS'])
            q_net = P_serv / (B * L)
            if q_net > q_all:
                continue
            s = calc_settlement_unimproved(P_serv, B, L, base_I, base_II, pdata['Es'])
            if s > 1.0:
                continue
            
            t_in, d_in, rho, b_size, b_space = design_footing_structural(Pu, B, L, cols[tag], pdata['fc'])
            cost = calc_foundation_cost(B, L, t_in, Df, rho, pdata['fc'], False)
            gov = 'BEARING' if q_net / q_all >= 0.80 else 'SETTLEMENT'
            best = {
                'foundation_type': 'SPREAD',
                'B_in': B_in, 'L_in': int(L * 12), 't_in': t_in, 'd_in': d_in,
                'bearing_stratum': 'I',
                'rho': round(rho, 4), 'bar_size': b_size, 'bar_spacing_in': b_space,
                'n_piers': 0, 'pier_diameter_in': 0, 'H_pier': 0,
                'Ra': 0.0, 'qg_psf': 0.0,
                'q_net': round(q_net, 2), 'q_all': round(q_all, 2), 's_tot': round(s, 3),
                'governing_constraint': gov,
                'cost': cost
            }
            if tag == 'W1':
                e_in, up_fs, sl_fs = check_w1_stability(pad, B, t_in)
                best['sliding_fs'] = sl_fs
                best['eccentricity_in'] = e_in
                best['uplift_fs'] = up_fs
            break
        footings[tag] = best
    
    # Check angular distortion between adjacent
    pairs = [('F1', 'F2', 24.0), ('F2', 'F3', 20.0), ('F3', 'F4', 16.0), ('F4', 'F5', 12.0), ('F5', 'W1', 5.0)]
    for t1, t2, span in pairs:
        ds = abs(footings[t2]['s_tot'] - footings[t1]['s_tot']) / 12.0
        dist = ds / span
        if dist > 1.0 / 500.0 and t1 == 'F5' and t2 == 'W1':
            for B_in in range(footings['W1']['B_in'] + 3, 480, 3):
                B = B_in / 12.0
                L = 24.0
                s = calc_settlement_unimproved(reactions[(pad, 'W1')]['SERVICE_D_PLUS_L']['P'], B, L, base_I, base_II, pdata['Es'])
                ds_new = abs(s - footings['F5']['s_tot'])
                if ds_new <= (span * 12.0 / 500.0) * 0.95:
                    t_in, d_in, rho, b_size, b_space = design_footing_structural(reactions[(pad, 'W1')]['STRENGTH_1.2D_1.6L']['P'], B, L, cols['W1'], pdata['fc'])
                    cost = calc_foundation_cost(B, L, t_in, Df, rho, pdata['fc'], False)
                    e_in, up_fs, sl_fs = check_w1_stability(pad, B, t_in)
                    footings['W1'] = {
                        'foundation_type': 'SPREAD',
                        'B_in': B_in, 'L_in': int(L * 12), 't_in': t_in, 'd_in': d_in,
                        'bearing_stratum': 'I',
                        'rho': round(rho, 4), 'bar_size': b_size, 'bar_spacing_in': b_space,
                        'n_piers': 0, 'pier_diameter_in': 0, 'H_pier': 0,
                        'Ra': 0.0, 'qg_psf': 0.0,
                        'q_net': round(reactions[(pad, 'W1')]['SERVICE_D_PLUS_L']['P'] / (B * L), 2),
                        'q_all': round(calc_qall(B, L, Df, pdata['Dw'], pdata['FS']), 2),
                        's_tot': round(s, 3),
                        'governing_constraint': 'ANGULAR_DISTORTION',
                        'cost': cost,
                        'sliding_fs': sl_fs, 'eccentricity_in': e_in, 'uplift_fs': up_fs
                    }
                    break
    pad_cost = sum(f['cost'] for f in footings.values())
    return footings, pad_cost

    t = t_in / 12.0
    L = 24.0
    t_wall = 1.0
    W_f = B_ft * L * t * 0.150
    W_s = max(0.0, (B_ft - t_wall)) * L * (Df - t) * 0.118
    
    r_ot = reactions[(pad, 'W1')]['SERVICE_D_PLUS_L_PLUS_W']
    P_serv = r_ot['P']
    Hx_serv = r_ot['Hx']
    My_serv = r_ot['My']
    V_ot = P_serv + W_f + W_s
    M_base = My_serv + Hx_serv * t
    e = M_base / V_ot
    e_in = e * 12.0
    
    r_up = reactions[(pad, 'W1')]['UPLIFT_W']
    P_up = abs(r_up['P'])
    P_dead = reactions[(pad, 'W1')]['DEAD_ONLY']['P']
    W_resist = 0.6 * (P_dead + W_f + W_s)
    fs_uplift = W_resist / P_up
    
    r_sl = reactions[(pad, 'W1')]['0.6D_PLUS_W']
    P_06D = r_sl['P']
    Hx_sl = r_sl['Hx']
    V_sl = P_06D + 0.6 * (W_f + W_s)
    
    delta = 2.0 / 3.0 * phi
    tan_delta = math.tan(delta)
    R_base = V_sl * tan_delta
    
    Kp = (math.tan(math.radians(45.0 + 13.0)))**2
    z1 = Df - t
    z2 = Df
    int_p = Kp * gamma_total * (z2**2 - z1**2) / 2.0 + 2.0 * c_soil * math.sqrt(Kp) * (z2 - z1)
    Pp = int_p * B_ft
    R_total = R_base + 0.5 * Pp
    fs_sliding = R_total / Hx_sl
    
    return round(e_in, 2), round(fs_uplift, 2), round(fs_sliding, 2)

def calc_foundation_cost(B_ft, L_ft, t_in, Df_ft, rho, fc_psi, is_improved, pier_count=0, pier_depth_ft=0):
    conc_prices = {3000: 182.0, 4000: 196.0, 4500: 211.0, 5000: 228.0}
    c_price = conc_prices[fc_psi]
    t_ft = t_in / 12.0
    v_conc_cf = B_ft * L_ft * t_ft
    v_conc_cy = v_conc_cf / 27.0
    cost_conc = v_conc_cy * c_price
    w_steel_lb = 2.0 * rho * v_conc_cf * 490.0
    cost_steel = w_steel_lb * 1.42
    v_exc_cf = (B_ft + 2.0) * (L_ft + 2.0) * Df_ft
    v_exc_cy = v_exc_cf / 27.0
    cost_exc = v_exc_cy * 38.0
    v_bf_cy = max(0.0, v_exc_cy - v_conc_cy)
    cost_bf = v_bf_cy * 46.0
    cost_piers = pier_count * pier_depth_ft * 28.0 if is_improved else 0.0
    cost_platform = (B_ft * L_ft / 9.0) * 2.40 if is_improved else 0.0
    total = cost_conc + cost_steel + cost_exc + cost_bf + cost_piers + cost_platform
    return total

# SIZING ENGINES
def size_improved_pad(pad):
    pdata = borings[pad]
    footings = {}
    for tag in ['F1', 'F2', 'F3', 'F4', 'F5', 'W1']:
        P_serv = reactions[(pad, tag)]['SERVICE_D_PLUS_L']['P']
        Pu = reactions[(pad, tag)]['STRENGTH_1.2D_1.6L']['P']
        sta = stations[tag]
        base_I = round(pdata['A'] + (pdata['B'] - pdata['A']) * (sta / 77.0), 1)
        base_II = round(base_I + pdata['II'], 1)
        
        min_B_in = 21 if tag == 'W1' else 24
        best = None
        for B_in in range(min_B_in, 360, 3):
            B = B_in / 12.0
            L = 24.0 if tag == 'W1' else B
            q_all = calc_qall(B, L, Df, pdata['Dw'], pdata['FS'])
            q_net = P_serv / (B * L)
            if q_net > q_all:
                continue
                
            found_pier_config = False
            for n in range(1, 40):
                Ra = (n * A_pier) / (B * L)
                if Ra > 0.65:
                    continue
                qg_psf = (q_net * 1000.0) * (ns / (1.0 + (ns - 1.0) * Ra))
                if qg_psf > 18000.0:
                    continue
                
                req_depth = max(8, int(math.ceil(base_I - Df + 1.0)))
                H_pier = min(25, max(8, req_depth))
                
                s_tot, s_uz, s_lz, Ra_val, qg_val = calc_settlement_improved(P_serv, B, L, n, H_pier, base_I, base_II, pdata['Es'], pdata['kg'])
                if s_tot <= 1.0:
                    t_in, d_in, rho, b_size, b_space = design_footing_structural(Pu, B, L, cols[tag], pdata['fc'])
                    cost = calc_foundation_cost(B, L, t_in, Df, rho, pdata['fc'], True, n, H_pier)
                    
                    gov = 'BEARING' if q_net / q_all >= 0.80 else 'SETTLEMENT'
                    
                    best = {
                        'foundation_type': 'IMPROVED_SPREAD',
                        'B_in': B_in, 'L_in': int(L * 12), 't_in': t_in, 'd_in': d_in,
                        'bearing_stratum': 'I',
                        'rho': round(rho, 4), 'bar_size': b_size, 'bar_spacing_in': b_space,
                        'n_piers': n, 'pier_diameter_in': 30, 'H_pier': H_pier,
                        'Ra': round(Ra, 3), 'qg_psf': round(qg_psf, 1),
                        'q_net': round(q_net, 2), 'q_all': round(q_all, 2), 's_tot': round(s_tot, 3),
                        'governing_constraint': gov,
                        'cost': cost
                    }
                    if tag == 'W1':
                        e_in, up_fs, sl_fs = check_w1_stability(pad, B, t_in)
                        best['sliding_fs'] = sl_fs
                        best['eccentricity_in'] = e_in
                        best['uplift_fs'] = up_fs
                    found_pier_config = True
                    break
            if found_pier_config:
                break
        footings[tag] = best
    pad_cost = sum(f['cost'] for f in footings.values()) + 9500.0 # modulus test
    return footings, pad_cost

def size_spread_pad(pad):
    pdata = borings[pad]
    footings = {}
    for tag in ['F1', 'F2', 'F3', 'F4', 'F5', 'W1']:

        min_B_in = 21 if tag == 'W1' else 24

        for B_in in range(min_B_in, 480, 3):

            q_all = calc_qall(B, L, Df, pdata['Dw'], pdata['FS'])

            if q_net > q_all:
                continue
            s = calc_settlement_unimproved(P_serv, B, L, base_I, base_II, pdata['Es'])
            if s > 1.0:
                continue
            
            t_in, d_in, rho, b_size, b_space = design_footing_structural(Pu, B, L, cols[tag], pdata['fc'])
            cost = calc_foundation_cost(B, L, t_in, Df, rho, pdata['fc'], False)
            gov = 'BEARING' if q_net / q_all >= 0.80 else 'SETTLEMENT'
            best = {
                'foundation_type': 'SPREAD',
                'B_in': B_in, 'L_in': int(L * 12), 't_in': t_in, 'd_in': d_in,

                'rho': round(rho, 4), 'bar_size': b_size, 'bar_spacing_in': b_space,

                'q_net': round(q_net, 2), 'q_all': round(q_all, 2), 's_tot': round(s, 3),

                'cost': cost
            }
            if tag == 'W1':
                e_in, up_fs, sl_fs = check_w1_stability(pad, B, t_in)
                best['sliding_fs'] = sl_fs
                best['eccentricity_in'] = e_in
                best['uplift_fs'] = up_fs
            break
        footings[tag] = best
    
    # Check angular distortion between adjacent
    pairs = [('F1', 'F2', 24.0), ('F2', 'F3', 20.0), ('F3', 'F4', 16.0), ('F4', 'F5', 12.0), ('F5', 'W1', 5.0)]

                L = 24.0
                s = calc_settlement_unimproved(reactions[(pad, 'W1')]['SERVICE_D_PLUS_L']['P'], B, L, base_I, base_II, pdata['Es'])
                ds_new = abs(s - footings['F5']['s_tot'])
                if ds_new <= (span * 12.0 / 500.0) * 0.95:
                    t_in, d_in, rho, b_size, b_space = design_footing_structural(reactions[(pad, 'W1')]['STRENGTH_1.2D_1.6L']['P'], B, L, cols['W1'], pdata['fc'])
                    cost = calc_foundation_cost(B, L, t_in, Df, rho, pdata['fc'], False)
                    e_in, up_fs, sl_fs = check_w1_stability(pad, B, t_in)
                    footings['W1'] = {
                        'foundation_type': 'SPREAD',
                        'B_in': B_in, 'L_in': int(L * 12), 't_in': t_in, 'd_in': d_in,
                        'bearing_stratum': 'I',
                        'rho': round(rho, 4), 'bar_size': b_size, 'bar_spacing_in': b_space,
                        'n_piers': 0, 'pier_diameter_in': 0, 'H_pier': 0,
                        'Ra': 0.0, 'qg_psf': 0.0,
                        'q_net': round(reactions[(pad, 'W1')]['SERVICE_D_PLUS_L']['P'] / (B * L), 2),
                        'q_all': round(calc_qall(B, L, Df, pdata['Dw'], pdata['FS']), 2),

                        'cost': cost,
                        'sliding_fs': sl_fs, 'eccentricity_in': e_in, 'uplift_fs': up_fs
                    }
                    break
    pad_cost = sum(f['cost'] for f in footings.values())
    return footings, pad_cost

Df = 3.5 # 42 in
phi_deg = 26.0
phi = math.radians(phi_deg)
c_soil = 0.25 # ksf
gamma_total = 118.0 / 1000.0
gamma_sub = (118.0 - 62.4) / 1000.0

Nq = (math.tan(math.radians(45.0 + phi_deg / 2.0)))**2 * math.exp(math.pi * math.tan(phi))
Nc = (Nq - 1.0) / math.tan(phi)
Ngamma = 1.5 * (Nq - 1.0) * math.tan(phi)

def calc_qall(B, L, Df, Dw, FS):
    if Dw >= Df:
        sigma_zD = gamma_total * Df
    else:
        sigma_zD = gamma_total * Dw + gamma_sub * (Df - Dw)
    if Dw >= Df + B:
        gamma_eff = gamma_total
    elif Dw <= Df:
        gamma_eff = gamma_sub
    else:
        d = Dw - Df
        gamma_eff = gamma_sub + (d / B) * (gamma_total - gamma_sub)
    k = Df / B if Df / B <= 1.0 else math.atan(Df / B)
    sq = 1.0 + (B / L) * math.sin(phi)
    sgamma = 1.0 - 0.4 * (B / L)
    sc = 1.0 + (B / L) * (Nq / Nc) * math.cos(phi)
    dq = 1.0 + 2.0 * k * math.tan(phi) * (1.0 - math.sin(phi))**2
    dc = 1.0 + k * ((1.0 - math.sin(phi))**2) * (Nq / Nc)
    dgamma = 1.0
    q_ult = c_soil * Nc * sc * dc + sigma_zD * Nq * sq * dq + 0.5 * gamma_eff * B * Ngamma * sgamma * dgamma
    q_all_net = (q_ult / FS) - sigma_zD
    return q_all_net

def calc_settlement_unimproved(P, B, L, base_I, base_II, Es):
    q_net = P / (B * L)
    z_max = max(4.0 * B, 40.0)
    H = 0.25
    n_layers = int(math.ceil(z_max / H))
    total_s = 0.0
    for i in range(n_layers):
        z_mid = (i + 0.5) * H
        if z_mid > z_max:
            break
        d_sigma = (q_net * B * L) / ((B + z_mid) * (L + z_mid))
        depth = Df + z_mid
        if depth <= base_I:
            E = Es['I']
        elif depth <= base_II:
            E = Es['II']
        else:
            E = Es['III']
        total_s += (d_sigma * H) / E
    return total_s * 12.0

D_pier = 2.5
A_pier = math.pi / 4.0 * D_pier**2
ns = 10.0

def calc_settlement_improved(P, B, L, n_piers, H_pier, base_I, base_II, Es, kg):
    q_net = P / (B * L)
    q_net_psf = q_net * 1000.0
    Ra = (n_piers * A_pier) / (B * L)
    qg_psf = q_net_psf * (ns / (1.0 + (ns - 1.0) * Ra))
    qg_psi = qg_psf / 144.0
    s_uz = qg_psi / kg
    
    z_max = max(4.0 * B, 40.0)
    H = 0.25
    n_layers = int(math.ceil(z_max / H))
    s_lz = 0.0
    for i in range(n_layers):
        z_mid = (i + 0.5) * H
        if z_mid < H_pier or z_mid > z_max:
            continue
        d_sigma = (q_net * B * L) / ((B + z_mid) * (L + z_mid))
        depth = Df + z_mid
        if depth <= base_I:
            E = Es['I']
        elif depth <= base_II:
            E = Es['II']
        else:
            E = Es['III']
        s_lz += (d_sigma * H) / E
    s_lz *= 12.0
    return s_uz + s_lz, s_uz, s_lz, Ra, qg_psf

def design_footing_structural(Pu_kips, B_ft, L_ft, col_in, fc_psi):
    Pu = Pu_kips * 1000.0
    B = B_ft * 12.0
    L = L_ft * 12.0
    qu = Pu / (B * L)
    phi_v = 0.75
    phi_f = 0.90
    fy = 60000.0
    
    for t_in in range(12, 120, 3):
        d = t_in - 4.0
        if col_in > 12.0:
            bo = 4.0 * (col_in + d)
            area_punch = (col_in + d)**2
            Vu_punch = qu * (B * L - area_punch)
            Vc_punch = 4.0 * math.sqrt(fc_psi) * bo * d
            if Vu_punch > phi_v * Vc_punch:
                continue
        cant = (B - col_in) / 2.0
        if cant > d:
            Vu_1way = qu * L * (cant - d)
            Vc_1way = 2.0 * math.sqrt(fc_psi) * L * d
            if Vu_1way > phi_v * Vc_1way:
                continue
        
        Mu = qu * L * (cant**2) / 2.0
        A_coeff = (phi_f * fy**2) / (1.7 * fc_psi * L)
        B_coeff = -phi_f * fy * d
        C_coeff = Mu
        disc = B_coeff**2 - 4.0 * A_coeff * C_coeff
        if disc < 0:
            continue
        As = (-B_coeff - math.sqrt(disc)) / (2.0 * A_coeff)
        rho_calc = As / (L * t_in)
        rho = max(rho_calc, 0.0018)
        
        bars = {4: 0.20, 5: 0.31, 6: 0.44, 7: 0.60, 8: 0.79, 9: 1.00}
        best_bar = 4
        best_spacing = 12
        for b_size in [8, 7, 6, 5, 4]:
            a_bar = bars[b_size]
            s_in = (a_bar * L) / (rho * L * t_in)
            if s_in <= 12.0 and s_in >= 4.0:
                best_bar = b_size
                best_spacing = int(math.floor(s_in))
                break
        return t_in, d, rho, best_bar, best_spacing
    return 12, 8.0, 0.0018, 4, 12

def check_w1_stability(pad, B_ft, t_in):
    t = t_in / 12.0
    L = 24.0
    t_wall = 1.0
    W_f = B_ft * L * t * 0.150
    W_s = max(0.0, (B_ft - t_wall)) * L * (Df - t) * 0.118
    
    r_ot = reactions[(pad, 'W1')]['SERVICE_D_PLUS_L_PLUS_W']
    P_serv = r_ot['P']
    Hx_serv = r_ot['Hx']
    My_serv = r_ot['My']
    V_ot = P_serv + W_f + W_s
    M_base = My_serv + Hx_serv * t
    e = M_base / V_ot
    e_in = e * 12.0
    
    r_up = reactions[(pad, 'W1')]['UPLIFT_W']
    P_up = abs(r_up['P'])
    P_dead = reactions[(pad, 'W1')]['DEAD_ONLY']['P']
    W_resist = 0.6 * (P_dead + W_f + W_s)
    fs_uplift = W_resist / P_up
    
    r_sl = reactions[(pad, 'W1')]['0.6D_PLUS_W']
    P_06D = r_sl['P']
    Hx_sl = r_sl['Hx']
    V_sl = P_06D + 0.6 * (W_f + W_s)
    
    delta = 2.0 / 3.0 * phi
    tan_delta = math.tan(delta)
    R_base = V_sl * tan_delta
    
    Kp = (math.tan(math.radians(45.0 + 13.0)))**2
    z1 = Df - t
    z2 = Df
    int_p = Kp * gamma_total * (z2**2 - z1**2) / 2.0 + 2.0 * c_soil * math.sqrt(Kp) * (z2 - z1)
    Pp = int_p * B_ft
    R_total = R_base + 0.5 * Pp
    fs_sliding = R_total / Hx_sl
    
    return round(e_in, 2), round(fs_uplift, 2), round(fs_sliding, 2)

def calc_foundation_cost(B_ft, L_ft, t_in, Df_ft, rho, fc_psi, is_improved, pier_count=0, pier_depth_ft=0):
    conc_prices = {3000: 182.0, 4000: 196.0, 4500: 211.0, 5000: 228.0}
    c_price = conc_prices[fc_psi]
    t_ft = t_in / 12.0
    v_conc_cf = B_ft * L_ft * t_ft
    v_conc_cy = v_conc_cf / 27.0
    cost_conc = v_conc_cy * c_price
    w_steel_lb = 2.0 * rho * v_conc_cf * 490.0
    cost_steel = w_steel_lb * 1.42
    v_exc_cf = (B_ft + 2.0) * (L_ft + 2.0) * Df_ft
    v_exc_cy = v_exc_cf / 27.0
    cost_exc = v_exc_cy * 38.0
    v_bf_cy = max(0.0, v_exc_cy - v_conc_cy)
    cost_bf = v_bf_cy * 46.0
    cost_piers = pier_count * pier_depth_ft * 28.0 if is_improved else 0.0
    cost_platform = (B_ft * L_ft / 9.0) * 2.40 if is_improved else 0.0
    total = cost_conc + cost_steel + cost_exc + cost_bf + cost_piers + cost_platform
    return total

# SIZING ENGINES
def size_improved_pad(pad):
    pdata = borings[pad]
    footings = {}
    for tag in ['F1', 'F2', 'F3', 'F4', 'F5', 'W1']:
        P_serv = reactions[(pad, tag)]['SERVICE_D_PLUS_L']['P']
        Pu = reactions[(pad, tag)]['STRENGTH_1.2D_1.6L']['P']
        sta = stations[tag]
        base_I = round(pdata['A'] + (pdata['B'] - pdata['A']) * (sta / 77.0), 1)
        base_II = round(base_I + pdata['II'], 1)
        
        min_B_in = 21 if tag == 'W1' else 24
        best = None
        for B_in in range(min_B_in, 360, 3):
            B = B_in / 12.0
            L = 24.0 if tag == 'W1' else B
            q_all = calc_qall(B, L, Df, pdata['Dw'], pdata['FS'])
            q_net = P_serv / (B * L)
            if q_net > q_all:
                continue
                
            found_pier_config = False
            for n in range(1, 40):
                Ra = (n * A_pier) / (B * L)
                if Ra > 0.65:
                    continue
                qg_psf = (q_net * 1000.0) * (ns / (1.0 + (ns - 1.0) * Ra))
                if qg_psf > 18000.0:
                    continue
                
                req_depth = max(8, int(math.ceil(base_I - Df + 1.0)))
                H_pier = min(25, max(8, req_depth))
                
                s_tot, s_uz, s_lz, Ra_val, qg_val = calc_settlement_improved(P_serv, B, L, n, H_pier, base_I, base_II, pdata['Es'], pdata['kg'])
                if s_tot <= 1.0:
                    t_in, d_in, rho, b_size, b_space = design_footing_structural(Pu, B, L, cols[tag], pdata['fc'])
                    cost = calc_foundation_cost(B, L, t_in, Df, rho, pdata['fc'], True, n, H_pier)
                    
                    gov = 'BEARING' if q_net / q_all >= 0.80 else 'SETTLEMENT'
                    
                    best = {
                        'foundation_type': 'IMPROVED_SPREAD',
                        'B_in': B_in, 'L_in': int(L * 12), 't_in': t_in, 'd_in': d_in,
                        'bearing_stratum': 'I',
                        'rho': round(rho, 4), 'bar_size': b_size, 'bar_spacing_in': b_space,
                        'n_piers': n, 'pier_diameter_in': 30, 'H_pier': H_pier,
                        'Ra': round(Ra, 3), 'qg_psf': round(qg_psf, 1),
                        'q_net': round(q_net, 2), 'q_all': round(q_all, 2), 's_tot': round(s_tot, 3),
                        'governing_constraint': gov,
                        'cost': cost
                    }
                    if tag == 'W1':
                        e_in, up_fs, sl_fs = check_w1_stability(pad, B, t_in)
                        best['sliding_fs'] = sl_fs
                        best['eccentricity_in'] = e_in
                        best['uplift_fs'] = up_fs
                    found_pier_config = True
                    break
            if found_pier_config:
                break
        footings[tag] = best
    pad_cost = sum(f['cost'] for f in footings.values()) + 9500.0 # modulus test
    return footings, pad_cost

def size_spread_pad(pad):
    pdata = borings[pad]
    footings = {}
    for tag in ['F1', 'F2', 'F3', 'F4', 'F5', 'W1']:
        P_serv = reactions[(pad, tag)]['SERVICE_D_PLUS_L']['P']
        Pu = reactions[(pad, tag)]['STRENGTH_1.2D_1.6L']['P']
        sta = stations[tag]
        base_I = round(pdata['A'] + (pdata['B'] - pdata['A']) * (sta / 77.0), 1)
        base_II = round(base_I + pdata['II'], 1)
        
        min_B_in = 21 if tag == 'W1' else 24
        best = None
        for B_in in range(min_B_in, 480, 3):
            B = B_in / 12.0
            L = 24.0 if tag == 'W1' else B
            q_all = calc_qall(B, L, Df, pdata['Dw'], pdata['FS'])
            q_net = P_serv / (B * L)
            if q_net > q_all:
                continue
            s = calc_settlement_unimproved(P_serv, B, L, base_I, base_II, pdata['Es'])
            if s > 1.0:
                continue
            
            t_in, d_in, rho, b_size, b_space = design_footing_structural(Pu, B, L, cols[tag], pdata['fc'])
            cost = calc_foundation_cost(B, L, t_in, Df, rho, pdata['fc'], False)
            gov = 'BEARING' if q_net / q_all >= 0.80 else 'SETTLEMENT'
            best = {
                'foundation_type': 'SPREAD',
                'B_in': B_in, 'L_in': int(L * 12), 't_in': t_in, 'd_in': d_in,
                'bearing_stratum': 'I',
                'rho': round(rho, 4), 'bar_size': b_size, 'bar_spacing_in': b_space,
                'n_piers': 0, 'pier_diameter_in': 0, 'H_pier': 0,
                'Ra': 0.0, 'qg_psf': 0.0,
                'q_net': round(q_net, 2), 'q_all': round(q_all, 2), 's_tot': round(s, 3),
                'governing_constraint': gov,
                'cost': cost
            }
            if tag == 'W1':
                e_in, up_fs, sl_fs = check_w1_stability(pad, B, t_in)
                best['sliding_fs'] = sl_fs
                best['eccentricity_in'] = e_in
                best['uplift_fs'] = up_fs
            break
        footings[tag] = best
    
    # Check angular distortion between adjacent
    pairs = [('F1', 'F2', 24.0), ('F2', 'F3', 20.0), ('F3', 'F4', 16.0), ('F4', 'F5', 12.0), ('F5', 'W1', 5.0)]
    for t1, t2, span in pairs:
        ds = abs(footings[t2]['s_tot'] - footings[t1]['s_tot']) / 12.0
        dist = ds / span
        if dist > 1.0 / 500.0 and t1 == 'F5' and t2 == 'W1':
            for B_in in range(footings['W1']['B_in'] + 3, 480, 3):
                B = B_in / 12.0
                L = 24.0
                s = calc_settlement_unimproved(reactions[(pad, 'W1')]['SERVICE_D_PLUS_L']['P'], B, L, base_I, base_II, pdata['Es'])
                ds_new = abs(s - footings['F5']['s_tot'])
                if ds_new <= (span * 12.0 / 500.0) * 0.95:
                    t_in, d_in, rho, b_size, b_space = design_footing_structural(reactions[(pad, 'W1')]['STRENGTH_1.2D_1.6L']['P'], B, L, cols['W1'], pdata['fc'])
                    cost = calc_foundation_cost(B, L, t_in, Df, rho, pdata['fc'], False)
                    e_in, up_fs, sl_fs = check_w1_stability(pad, B, t_in)
                    footings['W1'] = {
                        'foundation_type': 'SPREAD',
                        'B_in': B_in, 'L_in': int(L * 12), 't_in': t_in, 'd_in': d_in,
                        'bearing_stratum': 'I',
                        'rho': round(rho, 4), 'bar_size': b_size, 'bar_spacing_in': b_space,
                        'n_piers': 0, 'pier_diameter_in': 0, 'H_pier': 0,
                        'Ra': 0.0, 'qg_psf': 0.0,
                        'q_net': round(reactions[(pad, 'W1')]['SERVICE_D_PLUS_L']['P'] / (B * L), 2),
                        'q_all': round(calc_qall(B, L, Df, pdata['Dw'], pdata['FS']), 2),
                        's_tot': round(s, 3),
                        'governing_constraint': 'ANGULAR_DISTORTION',
                        'cost': cost,
                        'sliding_fs': sl_fs, 'eccentricity_in': e_in, 'uplift_fs': up_fs
                    }
                    break
    pad_cost = sum(f['cost'] for f in footings.values())
    return footings, pad_cost

# Cattail Run Data Campus - BIM foundation parameter standard (Rev. 2)

The foundation geometry parameter file is consumed directly by the Revit family generator.  It is a
single UTF-8 JSON object named `foundation_geometry.json` with this shape:

```json
{"project": {"campus_total_cost_usd": 0.0, "frost_depth_in": 0, "afi_100yr_F_days": 0},
 "pads": {"<PAD-ID>": {
     "bearing_depth_in": 0, "fs_bearing": 0.0, "occupancy_class": "...",
     "improved": false, "sulfate_pct": 0.0, "sulfate_exposure_class": "S0|S1|S2",
     "exposure_classes": ["..."], "fc_psi": 0, "max_wcm": 0.0, "dewatering_days": 0,
     "governing_constraint": "...",
     "foundations": {"<TAG>": {
         "foundation_type": "SPREAD|IMPROVED_SPREAD",
         "B_in": 0, "L_in": 0, "thickness_in": 0, "bearing_stratum": "I|II|III",
         "reinforcement_ratio": 0.0, "bar_size": 4, "bar_spacing_in": 12,
         "q_net_ksf": 0.0, "q_allow_net_ksf": 0.0, "settlement_in": 0.0,
         "pier_count": 0, "pier_diameter_in": 0, "pier_depth_ft": 0,
         "area_replacement_ratio": 0.0, "top_of_pier_stress_psf": 0.0,
         "governing_constraint": "..."}}}}}
```

Rules the generator enforces:

* every one of the six pads and every one of its six foundations must be present;
* `B_in`, `L_in`, `thickness_in` and `bearing_depth_in` are NUMBERS in inches, dimensioned to the
  nearest 3 in; `pier_depth_ft` is a whole number of feet; `pier_count` is a whole number;
* no `null` values anywhere; a spread footing carries zeros in the pier fields;
* `bearing_depth_in` is identical for every foundation on a pad and is repeated once at pad level;
* `governing_constraint` is one of `BEARING`, `SETTLEMENT`, `ANGULAR_DISTORTION`, `MIN_WIDTH`,
  `SLIDING`, `OVERTURNING`, `UPLIFT`, `PUNCHING_SHEAR`, `FROST`;
* the shear-wall foundation of each pad additionally carries `sliding_fs`, `eccentricity_in` and
  `uplift_fs`.

The ground-improvement plan is a separate JSON object named `ground_improvement_plan.json`:

```json
{"stress_concentration_ratio_ns": 0.0, "pier_diameter_in": 0,
 "rigs_mobilised": 0, "mobilisation_cost_usd": 0.0, "pads_improved": ["..."],
 "rig_assignments": {"RIG-1": ["<PAD-ID>", "..."]},
 "modulus_tests": {"<PAD-ID>": 0},
 "pads": {"<PAD-ID>": {"stiffness_modulus_pci": 0.0, "treatment_depth_ft": 0,
                       "total_pier_lf": 0.0}}}
```

`treatment_depth_ft` at pad level is the deepest treatment depth used on that pad.
